primary_cause: Rate-shock plus financial-sector panic. Fed emergency return to near-zero rates directly pressures brokers with spread income
secondary_factors: Recession fears. Forced deleveraging. Concern zero rates compress net interest revenue tied to client cash balances. No major Schwab-specific headline
store_description: Schwab looked more like a rate-sensitive financial than an idiosyncratic story. With the Fed cutting to 0-0.25% on March 15 and the S&P 500 halted after an 8% opening drop on March 16 SCHW's 9.8% fall is most plausibly explained by panic around earnings pressure from lower rates.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Starbucks said Mar 16 closing dine-in areas for at least two weeks in U.S. and Canada moving to to-go only. Already warned and shut 2000+ China stores
secondary_factors: Broad market crash. Worsening social-distancing measures. Fear North America would follow China-style disruption
store_description: On March 16 Starbucks said it would close dine-in areas across the U.S. and Canada for at least two weeks and go to to-go only confirming that the virus was no longer just a China problem for the chain. That landed on the same day the market was already in full panic mode.

primary_cause: Commercial aerospace demand shock. Collapse in air travel. Airlines seeking emergency aid after U.S. travel ban and COVID shutdowns
secondary_factors: General market crash. Fears around pending Raytheon/UTC combination exposure to civil aviation cycle. No major RTX headline Mar 13-16
store_description: Even without a direct RTX headline the commercial-aerospace read-through was brutal. Trump Europe travel ban airlines slashing schedules and airlines openly seeking emergency aid all pointed to a severe near-term collapse in aircraft demand and aftermarket activity.

primary_cause: Macro-driven selloff in cyclical semis tied to handset demand risk. Intensifying concern COVID would hit global smartphone demand and supply chains
secondary_factors: Supply-chain uncertainty. Indiscriminate tech liquidation. No QCOM-specific headline Mar 13-16
store_description: QCOM appears to have traded as a high-beta semiconductor name exposed to a sudden global consumer-electronics slowdown. The market was rapidly repricing 2020 handset volumes and supply-chain stability.

primary_cause: No major Philip Morris-specific item. Broad de-risking and international-consumer-staples exposure to global disruption
secondary_factors: Emerging-market and currency worries. Supply-chain uncertainty. Indiscriminate selling of defensive multinationals
store_description: PM's decline looks much larger than a typical defensive staple move suggesting investors were not treating it as a safe haven. With global mobility and cross-border trade under stress investors focused on international exposure FX risk and plain forced selling.

primary_cause: No major P&G-specific headline. Broad market liquidation. Held up better — staples relatively defensive. Smaller 4.9% drop
secondary_factors: None clearly company-specific in the window
store_description: PG's smaller 4.9% drop stands out because it underperformed less than most names. No stock-specific trigger. Looks like a defensive name getting pulled lower in a historic forced-selloff session.

primary_cause: No TMUS-specific headline Mar 13-16. Broad risk-off plus merger-execution uncertainty. Sprint merger pending but not yet closed
secondary_factors: Leverage concerns. Indiscriminate selling despite telecom relatively defensive profile
store_description: TMUS did not have an obvious same-window negative corporate headline. This looks mostly like market stress hitting a still-transformational merger story. In a session where investors were dumping levered or integration-sensitive names T-Mobile's pending Sprint combination likely amplified the downside.

primary_cause: Zero-rate shock to bank profitability. JPMorgan said Mar 15 would halt share buybacks and redirect capital toward lending. Fed cut to 0-0.25%
secondary_factors: Buyback suspension. Credit-loss fears. Recession risk. Marketwide panic. Toxic combination for bank sentiment — lower NIMs and management preparing for stress
store_description: JPM had both sector and company-specific reasons to fall. On March 15 it halted buybacks and the Fed simultaneously slashed rates to 0-0.25% a toxic combination for bank sentiment because it signaled both lower net interest margins and management preparing for stress.

primary_cause: Consumer-credit stress fears. Broader financial collapse zero-rate shock rapidly rising fear of consumer credit deterioration
secondary_factors: Funding and credit-card delinquencies risk. Recession panic. Financial-sector liquidation. No Reuters Capital One-specific headline
store_description: COF's much steeper drop versus diversified banks fits its business mix. Investors were rapidly repricing unemployment household stress and the risk that credit-card and consumer-lending losses would spike. Capital One was hit harder than names with less consumer-credit concentration.

primary_cause: Elective-procedure shutdown risk. Reuters Mar 16 reported U.S. hospitals postponing elective surgeries to free capacity for COVID patients. Directly relevant to da Vinci procedure volumes
secondary_factors: Hospital budget pressure. Marketwide tech and medtech selloff
store_description: This one had a clear fundamental read-through. As hospitals began suspending elective procedures investors immediately had reason to expect fewer robotic surgeries lower instrument usage and weaker near-term system demand.

primary_cause: Global growth and recession shock. Escalating global shutdowns and recession fears. No major CAT-specific item
secondary_factors: Commodity weakness. Capex fears. Supply-chain disruption risk
store_description: CAT typically trades as a clean proxy for global industrial activity so it did not need a company headline to fall. By March 16 investors were pricing a sharp drop in construction mining and energy capex.

primary_cause: Zero-rate shock plus recession-driven credit fears. Big U.S. banks including Citi suspended buybacks Mar 15. Fed cut to 0-0.25%
secondary_factors: Buyback suspension. Concern over global consumer and corporate exposures. Higher-beta profile and heavier international and credit-sensitive exposures
store_description: Citi's 19.3% fall was steeper than JPM's which fits its higher-beta profile and heavier concern around international and credit-sensitive exposures. The combination of the Fed emergency zero-rate move industry-wide buyback suspensions and a suddenly worsening global recession outlook was the main driver.

primary_cause: Portfolio look-through exposure to market crash. Violent collapse across financials industrials travel and consumer names
secondary_factors: Large bank holdings. Industrial exposure. Concern over insurance and investment portfolio marks. No Berkshire-specific item
store_description: Berkshire traded as a diversified macro vehicle. Investors were implicitly marking down its bank holdings economically sensitive operating businesses and public-equity portfolio all at once.

primary_cause: No major Bristol Myers-specific headline. Broad March 16 liquidation. Healthcare and pharma somewhat more defensive than financials or travel
secondary_factors: None clearly stock-specific in that window
store_description: BMY's move looks mostly non-idiosyncratic. In a session where even defensives sold off to raise cash Bristol Myers fell materially but no evidence of a company-specific catalyst driving the stock.

primary_cause: Asset-manager exposure to collapsing markets and client de-risking. Historic collapse in global markets threatens asset values fee bases and client risk appetite
secondary_factors: Liquidity stress. Redemption fears. Financial-sector contagion. No BLK-specific report Mar 13-16
store_description: BlackRock was essentially hit through its business model. When trillions in equity value disappear and liquidity strains spread across markets investors price in lower AUM-linked fees and tougher flows.

primary_cause: Collapse in global travel demand. Trump Europe travel restriction Mar 11. Airlines seeking emergency aid. Global travel restrictions escalating
secondary_factors: Rising cancellations. Refund risk. Fears of prolonged freeze in global leisure and business travel. No company-specific BKNG headline in exact 3-day window
store_description: Booking was an obvious casualty of the travel freeze. With the U.S. imposing European travel restrictions and airlines slashing capacity while calling for state support investors were repricing a severe near-immediate contraction in bookings and cancellations.

primary_cause: Zero-rate shock to custody and bank earnings plus sector panic. BNY Mellon affected by industrywide buyback suspension Mar 15 alongside Fed emergency rate cut to zero
secondary_factors: Buyback suspension. Generalized financial deleveraging. Rate compression and systemic stress as immediate earnings headwinds
store_description: BK traded with the financial complex after two clear negative signals: banks halted buybacks and the Fed cut to zero. Even though BNY Mellon is custody-heavy rather than a classic consumer lender the market treated rate compression and systemic stress as immediate earnings headwinds.

primary_cause: Bank earnings repricing from zero rates. Big U.S. banks including BofA suspended buybacks Mar 15. Fed cut to 0-0.25%
secondary_factors: Buyback halt. Recession and credit-loss fears. Broad market panic. BofA survey showed investors rushing to cash
store_description: BAC's selloff was fundamentally consistent with the bank-sector shock. Near-zero rates compress margins while the buyback suspension signaled management priority had shifted to conserving capital and supporting customers all as markets priced a deep recession.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Cash and liquidity fears on top of collapsing aviation market. Boeing already said Mar 11 would draw down $13.8B loan and freeze hiring/overtime. Airlines urgent appeals for government aid
secondary_factors: Ongoing 737 MAX crisis. Airline distress. Near-term liquidity stress and deeper damage to order and delivery outlook
store_description: BA had one of the clearest stock-specific negatives. Boeing was already preserving cash by drawing down its loan and freezing hiring and then the COVID shock crushed airline demand just as customers were seeking aid and slashing capacity.

primary_cause: Collapse in T&E spending expectations. Travel-ban and travel-collapse news directly relevant because AmEx heavily tied to travel and entertainment spend
secondary_factors: Consumer-credit worries. Broad financial-sector selloff. Airlines slashing routes and seeking emergency aid. No Reuters AXP-specific Mar 13-16 headline
store_description: AXP was hit by a particularly bad mix of catalysts: it traded like both a financial and a travel proxy. With the Europe travel ban airlines cutting capacity and recession fears rising investors had a strong reason to expect a sharp drop in billed business and a rise in credit stress.
